title: The rope that was never a snake
hookLine: a glint in the wet sand at low tide, and a shell that was a shell the whole time
carry: jnana: you are the atman, not the passing mind
tomorrow: the sky over a parking lot goes pale. a Vedic singer saw it too.
last: BHAKTI: LOVE IS ITS OWN FRUIT.

cards: Low tide, late afternoon. Something in the wet sand catches the sun and flashes, bright as a dropped coin. It's a shell.
Nothing about the shell changed when it was picked up. It was a shell the whole time. What changed was the seeing.
Shankara chose very nearly this picture to open his commentary on the Brahma Sutras. Today's summit sit climbs back to the last stretch of the lineage track: jnana, the path of knowing.

teach.b: Before he comments on a single line of the Brahma Sutras, Shankara writes a preface about that shell: mother-of-pearl taken for silver, one thing mistaken for another.
His teaching is that a mistake like this sits at the root of bondage: taking the body and the mind, which come and go, for the self, the atman, which doesn't.
Gaudapada, in his verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, gives the same kind of picture.

teach.h: THE ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.
teach.b: On a dim path, a rope is taken for a snake. The fear is real. The snake isn't.
What ends the fear isn't fighting the snake or running from it. It's seeing. When the rope is seen as rope, the snake doesn't leave.
It was never there. The Brahma Sutras themselves open with a word that sounds almost casual: now.

teach.h: NOW, THEN, THE WISH TO KNOW.
teach.b: Now, then, the wish to know Brahman. In his comment on the fourth sutra, Shankara says freedom isn't produced, the way a pot is made from clay. It's what is already so, uncovered, the way the shell was always a shell.
Gaudapada's last picture is a firebrand whirled in the dark, drawing circles that aren't there. Hold the stick still, and the circles stop.
From up here, jnana looks less like piling up information and more like a light coming on.
Ramanuja, whom the year also read, reads it differently: he holds the world and the selves in it as real, the body of God, not a mistake to be seen through.

But on the jnana track, the work is this: a bad grade, a mood, a hard week pass across you the way the snake passed across the rope. They aren't you. Look closely enough, and what frightened you turns out to be rope.

how: Students of Advaita Vedanta study the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras and Shankara's commentaries with a teacher, and pair the study with reflection and meditation on what the self is.

o: a vow to stop reading so the mind can be quiet
a look back from the top at jnana, the path of knowing
a list of facts to memorize before you can be free

games.q: the path of knowing — tap the pairs.
p: taken for a snake in the dim light
glints like silver in Shankara's preface
whirled, it draws circles that aren't there

s: in Gaudapada's picture, the light makes the snake leave
the snake doesn't leave; it was never there. the light only shows the rope.
Shankara says freedom is produced by effort, like a pot from clay
he says it's what is already so, uncovered.
Ramanuja, also read this year, holds the world and the self as real
not everyone on the path reads the rope and snake the way the jnana track does.

games.q: dusk, a garden path. a coil lies across the stones and your heart jumps. what ends the fear, in Gaudapada's picture?
o: bringing a light and seeing it's a rope.
games.why: seeing ends it. once the rope is seen, the snake doesn't run away. it was never there to begin with.

practice: Bring to mind one worry that has been coiled on your path lately, and instead of fighting it, look at it more closely, the way a flashlight would: what exactly is there, and what have you added in the dim light?
Stay with plain seeing for a while, then let the worry rest and rest as the one who sees; if you pray, ask for clear sight.

wordCard.voice: The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: jnana, the path of knowing, and the rope that was only ever rope. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: jñāna, knowing, the path of knowledge; pronunciation varies by region.

carryVoice: Your line: you are the atman, not the passing mind. Nothing about the shell changed; the seeing did. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 2.17–18 (the rope and the snake); 4.47–50 (the firebrand)
